# SK1130 — A character span is compared to a constant by a call

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`span.SequenceEqual("abc")` is `span is "abc"`: C# 11 matches a `ReadOnlySpan<char>` against a constant string directly.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | 11.0 |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

C# 11 added the one thing that made spans awkward to read — a `ReadOnlySpan<char>` or `Span<char>` can be matched against a constant string pattern, and the compiler lowers that to the very `MemoryExtensions.SequenceEqual` call the source was already making. So the call and the pattern are the same program, and only one of them composes: a pattern goes into a `switch` arm, joins an `or`, and negates as `is not` without the reader having to find the `!` in front of a long receiver. `bare.SequenceEqual("world") || bare.SequenceEqual("worldViewProjection")` is two calls where `bare is "world" or "worldViewProjection"` is one question.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
static bool IsTransform(ReadOnlySpan<char> name) =>
    name.SequenceEqual("world") || name.SequenceEqual("worldViewProjection");
```

Write:

```csharp
static bool IsTransform(ReadOnlySpan<char> name) =>
    name is "world" or "worldViewProjection";
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The receiver's own static type must already be `Span<char>` or `ReadOnlySpan<char>`, and that is a compiler requirement rather than caution.** `char[] a; a.SequenceEqual("abc")` binds to the same `MemoryExtensions` method through an implicit span conversion, but `a is "abc"` is **CS0029** — the pattern has no conversion step, so it is declined by reading `GetTypeInfo(receiver).Type` rather than the converted type. Measured against the compiler, not assumed. ⚠ **`Enumerable.SequenceEqual` is a different method with different behaviour, and this is the false-positive class that matters.** On a `string` receiver the call is LINQ over `IEnumerable<char>`, and a null receiver makes it throw `ArgumentNullException` where `s is "abc"` quietly returns `false` — compiled and run, not reasoned about. The rule therefore requires the resolved symbol to be `System.MemoryExtensions.SequenceEqual`, and the two-parameter overload only: the overload taking an `IEqualityComparer<T>` has no pattern spelling at all. ⚠ **The two spellings agree on every input, which is why the fix is safe.** Fourteen were compiled and run — an exact match, a longer and a shorter span, an empty span, `default(ReadOnlySpan<char>)`, a span over a null string, two sliced spans, a case difference, and a `Span<char>` from `stackalloc` — and the pattern and the call returned the same `bool` for all of them. The empty constant was checked separately because it is the one that could have split `default` from `""`, and it does not: both `is ""` and `SequenceEqual("")` are `true` for a default span. ⚠ **The constant is re-spelled from its own source text**, so a `const string` argument stays a `const string` in the pattern — a constant pattern accepts one — and a verbatim or raw literal keeps its escaping. A `"abc".AsSpan()` argument is unwrapped to `"abc"`, because the pattern takes the string and not the span. Anything whose value is not a compile-time non-null string is declined; there is no `is null` for a span. ⚠ **The receiver must be a primary expression**, because the rewrite moves it from an argument position, where every precedence is legal, to the left of a relational operator, where most are not — this bites only the `MemoryExtensions.SequenceEqual(x, "abc")` static spelling, since a receiver of a member access is already primary. `!span.SequenceEqual("abc")` becomes `span is not "abc"` as one edit rather than leaving a `!` in front of a pattern. ⚠ The rule is silent below C# 11 — **CS8936**, confirmed by compiling it — and in every expression position where an `is` would need parentheses the author did not write. A comment or a preprocessor directive inside the replaced span withdraws the finding. Generated code is excluded.
